implementation_notes: Scala has no lock-free collections of its own; on the JVM the answer is java.util.concurrent (ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedDeque), all of which are the audited implementations. Scala's own contribution is structural: immutable case classes plus an AtomicReference and a CAS retry loop is a clean, correct lock-free structure, because retrying is free when the value is immutable - the CAS either succeeds with the new snapshot or you re-read and try again, and no node is ever mutated in place so ABA cannot arise. That composition (immutable state + atomic pointer) is the most maintainable way to get non-blocking behaviour in Scala and is worth reaching for before any hand-written queue. Scala.js has no shared memory across workers, and Scala Native uses the JVM-compatible collections.
idiom_name: immutable snapshot + AtomicReference CAS loop (the Scala-shaped answer); java.util.concurrent for structures
pitfalls: @tailrec is required for the retry loop; without it a long contention chain grows the stack.
The value in the AtomicReference must be immutable - a mutable case class makes the retry unsafe and reintroduces ABA.
Scala.js has no SharedArrayBuffer, so the worker-shared-memory variants do not apply on that target.
A single AtomicReference is a single contended cache line - under high write contention, sharding by key beats the elegance.
alternative: java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap / ConcurrentLinkedQueue, or an immutable snapshot published through AtomicReference
